Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 30 November 2023 at 10.00am
(Day 004)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning. Yes, Mr Muston.
MR MUSTON: Good morning, Commissioner.
I think the first thing we need to do is, there is an
update to the tender bundle, can I hand up to you what is
described as a further index to volume 7 and I tender the
documents listed there, for present purposes, at least, the
most important of which is document A53,
[MOH.9999.0005.0001], which is the joint report of Mr Alfa
D'Amato and Ms Deb Willcox.
THE COMMISSIONER: Those exhibits just have the number
already allocated to them.
EXHIBIT #A53-A65 BULK TENDER OF DOCUMENTS MARKED A53 TO A65
AS IDENTIFIED IN TENDER LIST
MR MUSTON: Thank you.
That, I think, brings us to today's evidence, which is
to be given as a joint session again by Ms Willcox and
Mr D'Amato.
Ms Willcox is probably still bound by the affirmation
she made two days ago, but Mr D'Amato might need to --
THE COMMISSIONER: Are we saying your name, correctly,
sir, is it D'Amato?
MR D'AMATO: D'Amato.
THE COMMISSIONER: That's the only error he'll make all
day.
<ALFA D'AMATO, sworn: [10.03am]
<DEBORAH WILLCOX, on former affirmation: [10.03am]
MR MUSTON: Can I just start by making sure I've got
a proper understanding of the evidence that has been given
over the last two days, Ms Willcox, at least insofar as
you're concerned.
I gather from the evidence that has been given that
there are, in essence, three important objectives that the
health system needs to be pursuing, no doubt amongst

others, but three important objectives, and they are,
first, an increase in focus on preventative health care; is
that right?
MS WILLCOX: Correct, yes.
MR MUSTON: Just in relation to that, to make sure we're
all dealing with the same thing, could you just give me
your very rough definition of what preventative health care
comprises?
MS WILLCOX: Yes, certainly. When we talk about
preventative health care or health promotion, we talk about
those services or activities that go to maintaining the
health and wellbeing of individuals in an attempt to avoid
them developing disease or requiring hospitalisation for
injury or otherwise.
Health promotion activities - and certainly health
prevention - goes to areas obviously important in
population health protection, such as vaccination, and
health promotion activities go towards management of
obesity, diet, exercise, falls prevention. So it's quite
a broad house, but in the main, it is about trying to
maintain the health and wellbeing of the population.
MR MUSTON: Thank you. So when we refer to preventative
health throughout the day today, it may be taken that that
broad house is what we're referring to.
MS WILLCOX: Thank you.
MR MUSTON: That's the first objective. The second
objective, as I understand it, is an increased delivery of
care in the community.
MS WILLCOX: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And that, in a way, is a role which has
traditionally been primarily played by the primary health
sector; is that right?
MS WILLCOX: Correct, and probably historically also
through home nursing and community nursing. That's
probably, too, a longstanding community-based activity.
MR MUSTON: The objective there is to deliver care in a

way which, as best as possible, avoids hospital
presentation, unless it's absolutely necessary.
MS WILLCOX: That's correct. Our objective always is to
ensure a person gets the right level of care at the right
place at the right time, and for many people, care in the
home or a community setting is appropriate, when it's based
on clinical judgment.
MR MUSTON: But there will still remain, obviously enough,
a need to deliver acute care in a hospital setting?
MS WILLCOX: Indeed.
MR MUSTON: The aim is to ensure that the people who are
presenting and receiving that care are only those who
genuinely need it?
MS WILLCOX: That's a perfect characterisation.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the way in which health care
across the board is delivered, the third objective which
I've drawn from the evidence is the need to move towards
allocative efficiency in the funding or as a driver of
health spending.
MS WILLCOX: That would be correct. The term "allocative
efficiency" is an approach that goes to drive equity of
access across our populations and communities as opposed to
a technical formulation of what sort of funding is
required.
MR MUSTON: Would I be right in my understanding that that
essentially means we need to be driven by a need to produce
the best health outcomes, allocative efficiency, as opposed
to technical efficiency, which is the most cost-effective
delivery of services and activity where it's delivered?
MS WILLCOX: Yes, that's correct. The approach is more
towards volume than outcome.
MR MUSTON: I certainly don't suggest that the evidence
that has been given over the past two days tells us that we
should not also be focusing on technical efficiency --
MS WILLCOX: Indeed.

MR MUSTON: -- where activity is required, but in terms of
the overall funding package, I gather, the objective is we
ought be trying to use that money to produce the best
health outcomes possible as our key objective.
MS WILLCOX: Yes, indeed.
THE COMMISSIONER: You reach a point where gains in
technical efficiency are pretty hard once you're highly
technically efficient.
MS WILLCOX: That is true. We're constantly, in the
system, looking for ways how we can increase our
efficiency. Some of those things go to, which Mr D'Amato
will no doubt talk to, some of our corporate back of house
activities, as tight as you can possibly gain, so you can
maximise your investment at the front for clinical care.
But there probably is at some point a limiting factor.
MR MUSTON: Having made sure my understanding of the
evidence that has been given so far is correct, I should
probably move to this next point, which is just to identify
Mr D'Amato, your role within NSW Health. You are the
deputy secretary financial services and asset management.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: That's a role you have held since April 2021.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: I think you have been working broadly within
the health sector since at least March 2009 according to
your CV.
MR D'AMATO: Yes, that's correct.
MR MUSTON: I won't invite you to tell us or to list all
of your previous experience in the New South Wales health
system, but I assume that the recent experience which is
described in the CV, which is at [MOH.9999.0006.0001],
accurately reflects that history and experience.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Coming back to these three important
objectives that we've identified from the evidence given so

far, those objectives need to be pursued against the
background of the challenges that the two of you have
identified in paragraphs 77 to 92 of your joint report,
which is at document [MOH.9999.0005.0001], commencing at
page 16. Perhaps if that could be brought up.
We are dealing with the answers that you have given to
question 6 there. I don't need you to go through them in
detail but there's just a couple that I wouldn't mind
hearing you develop. The first is do you see paragraph 87,
at the foot of that page, where you refer to one of the
challenges being faced by the health system and the funding
of health going forward being the introduction of new
technologies. Could I just ask you to develop that a
little bit? What are the technologies, first of all?
MS WILLCOX: The evolution of specialised technologies is
moving very rapidly, and there are new drugs and tests and
procedures that are, as I say, evolving constantly in the
health system.
We want to provide the very best care to our patients
and give them the opportunity to receive the latest
treatments and drugs and technologies to maximise their
recovery or wellbeing, but some of them come at a very
large cost and we need to make sure that our processes
within the ministry, working with our clinicians and other
partners, are such that we can make an appropriate judgment
call about what the system is able to provide.
Our role is to provide services to the entire
community, and there are examples where, for instance, some
of these ground-breaking medications can be in the millions
of dollars for an individual patient. That's not to make
a judgment that that individual is not worth it; it's just
to give some perspective on the quantum of some of these
new medications and some of the technologies - as to what
their value is.
MR MUSTON: What is the process around decision-making in
terms of a new treatment? Let's say there's a new
treatment that has become available which is revealed to be
very effective, but it's also very, very expensive. What's
the process internally in terms of decision-making as to
whether to offer it through the public health system?
MS WILLCOX: We have an expert group that is designed to

assess what's coming forward so that we can make a judgment
on the evidence and the outcomes associated with
a particular device or medication.
There are Commonwealth pathways as well. But for us
internally, we look at the evidence, what is the
appropriateness, is there a research context from which
this new drug or technology has come forward? We want to
evaluate it against the priorities of the system as well,
whether that be value-based health care, priority
conditions, such as dementia, heart disease, whatever the
key conditions that we know to be creating the greatest
impact on the system, so there is a reference back to some
of those priorities in order to support a decision or not.
MR MUSTON: Dealing with that decision-making process, to
what extent does the cost of the particular medication or
treatment factor in to that decision-making? I think
a moment ago you told us that some of them can be up to
$1 million per patient. That's a large amount of money.
MS WILLCOX: Yes.
MR MUSTON: How does that $1 million per patient factor
figure into decision-making about whether or not to offer
the treatment through the public health system?
MS WILLCOX: It's obviously a complex ethical question.
The circumstances for which that may arise have been fairly
infrequent, it would be fair to say. In the most recent
times, both Mr D'Amato and I have been involved in two
patients who required, or were indicated they required,
a very expensive medication, they were at end stage of
their condition and had exhausted all other treatments, and
a decision was made to fund those particular medications
for those individuals.
We could only but suspect there will be more of this
over time, and so we're working with the Commonwealth
around this, who are partners in the funding for some of
these new technologies and treatments that are coming on
board.
The main group of things that come forward to us for
consideration ultimately end up in the pathway of not
agreeing to because the evidence is not in, or the
requisite value is not apparent, or they may be things that

then we decide to fund as part of a statewide service, so
things like CAR T cell therapy may be one example, where
there's a lot of evidence, a lot of research, agreement
within the ministry and with the appropriate clinical
advice, and that is now factored in to a service agreement
with a funding approach.
MR MUSTON: We might come back to the way the funding
approach works but, for present purposes, I gather the
reason that the new technologies or the emergence of new
technologies is a challenge to the funding of health is
because they can be very expensive.
MS WILLCOX: Yes.
MR MUSTON: So they make delivering health care more
expensive in individual patient cases than it once was?
MS WILLCOX: Indeed.
MR MUSTON: Could I ask you to turn over the page to - do
you see there paragraph 90? That is another challenge that
you've identified, which is the impact of capital
investment on recurrent funding. At the end of the
paragraph there, you refer to a significant future capital
pipeline.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: I'll come back to just how all of that impacts
from a budgeting perspective, but can I just ask at this
stage, what is the significant future capital pipeline that
you're referring to in paragraph 90?
MR D'AMATO: Sure. As documented in the budget papers,
the government has announced a pipeline of capital for
health of around 13.8 billion, and this is in one of the
documents that was published in September. Included in the
13.8 billion, there is an amount that has been established
for new works or new announced capital projects that will
be delivered within the next four years, as well as
projects that will be completed, that were previously
announced but that will be completed in the four years
coming.
As well as, if you want, new buildings, in the
13.8 billion we need to acknowledge there's also a spend

for ICT, for instance, IT programs, so we have a big
investment in single digital patient record, which is also
captured as capital spend.
So that is what is the pipeline, and to just mention
what we have estimated in regards to that pipeline and the
impact of those that are due to be completed within the
next four years, we expect to see around 800 additional
inpatient beds coming on line in 2025/26, and our estimate
is that to operate this additional capacity we will require
around 220 million. That's estimated only starting from
1 July.
So we know that there are different assumptions that
we need to test between now and then, but we are keeping
always a close eye. We always focus on what is in the
forwards and risks associated with the financial impact on
the recurrent side of our budget.
MR MUSTON: So again, to make sure I have understood it,
the pipeline involves some projects which are not bricks
and mortar projects?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Like the single patient record?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: That's an IT project. But also traditional
bricks and mortar projects like building a new hospital
facility or upgrading an existing hospital facility?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct. And I just want to stress
that both will have an impact on our recurrent - even IT
projects will have an impact on our recurrent operating
expenses, mainly because of the nature of the new IT
programs which are all as a service.
MR MUSTON: The last one I wanted to ask you very quickly
about was if you look at paragraph 91, I just wonder, you
see there you've said:
There is a strong need for more equitable
sharing of risk and cost across the
Commonwealth and NSW in provision of health
services.

What do you mean by that?
MR D'AMATO: The main risk that we want to highlight in
this paragraph is the fact that there is a delay between
the data collected to inform the national efficient price,
which is data collected from all our hospitals in ABF
terms, and all other hospitals, ABF hospitals, across the
nation, and provided to an Independent Health and Aged Care
Pricing Authority once a year.
What the delay is, is around three years. The data
that informed this year's national efficient price would
have been informed from data that was from three years ago,
which probably barely accounted for COVID cost and barely
reflected the inflation impact that we are witnessing right
now. So that is a risk that we called out several times
with IHACPA, and the challenge is that it's difficult for
them to collect across the nation all this data in a timely
fashion so they can inform the national efficient price,
but there is a risk.
MR MUSTON: I will come back to the way the Commonwealth
delivers its funding, but just so I can make sure I've
understood what you've said, the challenge that you're
identifying there is, in effect, the fact that the way in
which the Commonwealth's contribution to the funding of
health care is quantified involves an assessment of past
delivery and the cost of delivering services in the past,
and that's failing to keep up, potentially, with the
ever-increasing cost of delivering those services?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MS WILLCOX: I might add, Mr Muston - and Mr D'Amato may
wish to elaborate - the other risk around it is what's in
scope, and as we see the change in the population needs and
the profile of disease, and to your earlier comments about
prevention and community-based care, the scope of those
things that fit within the IHACPA model is narrow,
potentially, there's a narrowing of that which creates
a risk for us in terms of what the state then needs to
fund.
MR MUSTON: Maybe I'll ask you to develop that a little
bit further. Is part of that the fact that the second of
our objectives, delivering health care outside of the

hospital setting in a way that ideally prevents hospital
presentations or minimises hospital presentations, is
traditionally the domain of the Commonwealth funded primary
health sector?
MS WILLCOX: Correct.
MR MUSTON: And is the scope creep that you are talking
about there referable to the fact that, as the state
expands its services or adjusts its services to secure that
objective through its own spending, it is, in effect,
picking up care which would traditionally have been
delivered through a Commonwealth funded aspect of the
health service?
MS WILLCOX: In part, but possibly the more significant
area is that as we work to try and ensure people, as
I said, get their care at the right place - and not always
is a hospital the right place - we have adapted our models
of care and our ability to care for people in the community
through virtual care, home monitoring, self-management,
a whole raft of things, in order to ensure people stay out
of hospital.
It's not, strictly speaking, in a GP practice,
although that relationship with the GP and primary care is
critical, but we have made a positive move to try and avoid
people coming into hospital, and we find ourselves sort of
straddled, I guess, between the acute services of the state
system and primary care. So there's a growing portion in
the middle where the risk potentially sits that we would
like to work with our colleagues in the Commonwealth to see
how we can get a more equitable sharing of that financial
cost.
MR MUSTON: And so again we'll come to activity based
funding in a moment, but is the issue that you've just
described the fact that the way in which the Commonwealth's
contribution through activity based funding is measured, by
the coding and recognition of activity, doesn't actually,
at the moment, recognise that activity which is delivered
outside of the hospital setting that you are expanding into
in order to achieve the second of those objectives?
MS WILLCOX: Yes.
MR D'AMATO: That's right, you are correct. I think the

core issue is again the delay from the independent
authority to recognise innovation in the service delivery,
if you want, because this agency is tasked to determine the
scope of services in then attracting, if you want,
Commonwealth contribution. This service can be delivered
from block funded service, those small hospitals, as well
as ABF hospitals.
But that fact is that when we step into innovative
solutions, as Ms Willcox described, it's challenging for us
to attract immediately, if you want, the additional funding
from the Commonwealth, because we have to go through
a process to demonstrate that these are services that
otherwise would have been provided in other settings, being
hospital settings, or already deemed to be in scope for the
Commonwealth. So that's the challenge for us. There is
a gap, if you want; there's a challenge in the process in
us accelerating some of this innovative service delivery.
MR MUSTON: There are two buckets, as it were, a bucket
which is traditional primary health care delivered through
the Medicare system. There's a bucket which is traditional
hospital based health care delivered traditionally in
hospitals, funded in part by the state and in part by the
Commonwealth, but as you expand your services to keep
people out of hospital, there is a gap between those
buckets that you've identified, which means the state, to
provide those services, is meeting the full cost of them
unless and until such time as an agreement is reached with
the Commonwealth to change the way the funding of the
hospital-based treatment is measured to, in effect, pick
that up.
MS WILLCOX: Yes, that's a correct characterisation,
Mr Muston. There are about five significant innovative
models of care that have been developed in the state system
in recent times that Mr D'Amato was referring to, RPA
virtual being one, the frailty collaborative commissioning
work that was undertaken in Northern Sydney.
Our colleagues in the Commonwealth understand the
technical barriers around this and we work closely with
them, but it did take a considerable period of time and now
the Commonwealth, based on the evidence, have agreed to in
part fund those particular innovations. But I guess it
just reinforces the point that the pace at which the
innovation and evolution of care is happening in the

system, the technical part of the system and the funding
part of the system can't keep up or move at the same pace.
MR MUSTON: I should probably ask this now: do you
perceive that that delay between the technical innovation
and funding catching up with it is actually preventing
innovation from occurring?
MS WILLCOX: I think our clinicians on the ground just
naturally continue to innovate, so I think it would have no
impact on their desire to constantly look and see what they
can do to improve care.
I think we progress regardless, is what I would say.
We've done many, I think, really clever and insightful
innovations in care, just even in the last couple of years
and certainly through COVID, it really stands out. So
I don't think it hampers us. It's more an issue probably
for people like myself and Mr D'Amato to make sure that we
can work with our Commonwealth colleagues and see if we can
secure the appropriate funding. But I don't think it stops
us all collectively believing that we need to keep evolving
and progressing and innovating.
MR MUSTON: Mr D'Amato.
MR D'AMATO: I think that is absolutely right. What it
does, though, is it at times prevents us from scaling
innovative solutions statewide, because we have to go
through this iterative process to determine whether we have
an opportunity to then access additional funding, and it
might take two years, and then to determine whether we can,
if you want, expand across the state.
THE COMMISSIONER: Does that mean there is some innovation
that seems to work really well - let's call it RPA virtual,
it doesn't matter what it is - but because of the long
period of time of dealing with the Commonwealth to secure
funding for it, there's a delay in expanding something that
you might already think, "This is going to work and it
should be scaled out"; it's the delay? As you said, it's
not the delay in the clinicians working towards innovation;
it's the delay in expanding it until you can make sure it
can be paid for.
MS WILLCOX: That's correct, yes.

MR MUSTON: That's probably a useful point for us to move
into the funding arrangements. You've told us in a very
high level at paragraphs 4 and 5 of your report that health
operates in a complex funding environment - that's probably
an understatement - and that the New South Wales public
health care is funded primarily by the New South Wales and
Australian governments with additional funding received
from direct source revenue such as private health insurance
payments and individual payments.
Can I just ask you at a very general level at this
stage to explain what those key funding sources are?
I understand what you tell us there, that there's the
Commonwealth Government, there's state government and then
there are the other sources like private health insurance,
but what are the actual mechanisms by which that funding is
provided? Start with the Commonwealth.
MR D'AMATO: Sure. So the appropriation, being the state
funding component of our budget which reflects around
60 per cent, includes normally - and this is what is
documented in the budget papers - the capital component,
the spend, and the recurrent component.
MR MUSTON: Just pausing there, the Commonwealth
contributes to both the capital and the recurrent component
of the funding?
MR D'AMATO: The Commonwealth, through the NHRA,
contributes only towards recurrent, only towards operating
expenses.
MR MUSTON: Let's start with the Commonwealth contribution
to the funding. We've heard about the ABF funding. How is
the Commonwealth contributing to the funding of health care
in New South Wales?
MR D'AMATO: So the main vehicle is through the NHRA, the
National Health Reform Agreement. Through that vehicle
there are two main drivers. There's either ABF or it's
through a block funded arrangement.
The block funded arrangement can further split into
two components, such as small hospitals, or it can be a
different block funding arrangement such as teaching,
training and research; it could be specialist services like
mental health, forensic mental health. These are

determined based on historical costs.
The bulk of the payment, being from the Commonwealth
under the NHRA, is around 8.2 billion for this financial
year. Of that, 7 billion is related to activity based
funding activity. In setting this 7 billion, the
Commonwealth takes into account three aspects: one is the
base, and this is all documented in the National Health
Reform Agreement; then to the base adds what is then
reflected to be the price changes, and this is determined
from the national efficient price, which we all
contribute - we, as in all states and territories,
contribute - data on an annual basis; and then the final
part is the volume.
The volume reflects what we, as each individual state
and territory, provide to the administrator of the health
funding body on a yearly basis, normally around March, as
a high-level estimate, and then we update end of May what
is going to be the activity throughput that we are
targeting to deliver in the following financial year.
These are --
MR MUSTON: The activity that you are reporting on is
treatment delivered in hospitals and out of hospitals to
the extent that it is captured by the existing codes that
have been identified as things that the Commonwealth will
contribute towards the funding?
MR D'AMATO: That's right. It will be activity deemed to
be in-scope, and as we mentioned before, the Independent
Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority will determine the
scope of services.
MR MUSTON: So in relation to that, am I right in assuming
that the ABF side of the funding is primarily driven by and
directed towards the funding of hospitals and expansion of
scope in and around hospitals to provide what is
essentially acute care?
MR D'AMATO: Yes, acute care, definitely. I think that
it's fair to note that the second area of funding is
directed towards what we call "non-admitted patient care",
so there could be activity delivered from hospital
settings, providing it is of a clinical intent, or it could
be provided from other settings, so it could be from
a community health centre, if it is a nurse --

MR MUSTON: What sort of care would that be? What's an
example of that?
MR D'AMATO: It could be nurse-led clinics, it could be
allied health clinics. It could be hospital avoiders. It
could be hospital in the home, perhaps, if it is under
a certain model, where the nurses or teams are sitting
perhaps outside the hospital as a footprint, and delivering
care to patients in their home.
MR MUSTON: To the extent that you have previously been
able to negotiate with the Commonwealth Government about it
contributing towards the payment of those services through
the identification of a code that captures them?
MR D'AMATO: Yes. I think that the other components to
reflect on is that the activity based funding is based on
a classification. We call it streams. Whether it's acute
settings, whether it's sub-acute, mental health or
non-admitted, they each have a particular classification,
so that then the services can be described in an homogenous
way and therefore then funded according to a price, that is
set by the independent authority.
MR MUSTON: So in relation to preventative health that
we've talked about, to what extent, or in what way, is the
Commonwealth contributing to the funding of preventative
health in the state?
MR D'AMATO: In terms of prevention, the way it has been
described, particularly in regards to elements around
health promotion, there is not a direct funding link to the
activity based funding. Through the National Health Reform
Agreement we do receive around 160 million a year for what
is described in the budget papers, the Commonwealth budget
papers, as "public health", and some of these funds will go
towards supporting some of these interventions.
MR MUSTON: Is that delivered as block funding?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Is that block funding tied to the preventative
health measures?
MR D'AMATO: It does contribute towards the health

promotion and public health, yes, but there has been an
historical arrangement that there is - if you want, despite
the fact it is capturing in the payment that flows to us
through the National Health Reform Agreement, there is no
formula or no opportunities for us to renegotiate that
amount.
MR MUSTON: But I guess my question is: having received
that amount, are you bound by the agreement to spend it on
preventative health or is it just contributed to the
overall budget?
MR D'AMATO: It's contributed towards the overall budget.
But we spend more than what we receive from the
Commonwealth on preventative health. Around 4 per cent of
our budget is spent on public health, health promotion,
screening, so on.
MR MUSTON: So that 4 per cent is contributed to by the
$100 million you have told us about that the Commonwealth
gives you as a block for public health?
MR D'AMATO: That's right, yes.
MR MUSTON: In terms of preventative health, I think,
Ms Willcox, you referred to vaccination or immunisation
programs.
MS WILLCOX: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Is that captured by that block or is that
contributed to by the Commonwealth in any way?
MS WILLCOX: There is program funding, but, Mr D'Amato,
it is probably one for you.
MR D'AMATO: Yes, that's probably a bit of a complex area
because there is a national partnership agreement in
regards to immunisation and vaccination, so depending on
which program we're talking about, there will be some
elements that the Commonwealth might be involved directly
with us, so essential vaccine is one of these programs that
come to my mind. These arrangements are renegotiated on
a regular basis, but again, it depends on which
intervention we're talking about. Normally, it would be
most likely outside the National Health Reform Agreement.

MR MUSTON: So entirely separate to the National Health
Reform Agreement there may be separate agreements,
depending on the particular vaccine we're talking about?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: I guess two examples that we're all familiar
with are the COVID vaccine and the flu vaccine.
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Are they captured by an arrangement with the
Commonwealth outside of the National Health Reform
Agreement?
